metrics.label: Population
metrics.question: Which country has a larger population?
metrics.definition: Total population, using the midyear estimate. Counts residents regardless of citizenship or legal status.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Total population is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship. The values shown are midyear estimates.

metrics.label: Population density
metrics.question: Which country has more people per square kilometer?
metrics.definition: Midyear population divided by land area in square kilometers. Land area excludes inland water bodies.
metrics.sourceName:
FAO population estimates, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO);
World Bank population estimates, World Bank (WB), publisher: World Bank (WB)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Population density is midyear population divided by land area in square kilometers. Population is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship--except for refugees not permanently settled in the country of asylum, who are generally considered part of the population of their country of origin. Land area is a country's total area, excluding area under inland water bodies, national claims to continental shelf, and exclusive economic zones. In most cases the definition of inland water bodies includes major rivers and lakes.

metrics.label: Forest coverage
metrics.question: Which country has a larger share of forest?
metrics.definition: Forest area as a percentage of land area. Includes natural and planted forests; excludes agricultural tree stands and urban parks.
metrics.sourceName: FAOSTAT, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), uri: https://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/RL, publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Forest area (% of land area) is the share of total land area that is under natural or planted stands of trees of at least 5 meters in situ, whether productive or not, and excludes tree stands in agricultural production systems (for example, in fruit plantations and agroforestry systems) and trees in urban parks and gardens.

metrics.label: Urban population
metrics.question: Where does a larger share of people live in urban areas?
metrics.definition: People living in urban areas as a percentage of total population. Urban areas follow each country’s national definition.
metrics.sourceName: World Urbanization Prospects, United Nations (UN), uri: https://population.un.org/wup/, note: United Nations Population Division's World Urbanization Prospects, National definitions, publisher: UN Population Division
metrics.sourceDefinition: Urban population refers to people living in urban areas as defined by national statistical offices. The data are collected and smoothed by United Nations Population Division.

metrics.label: Internet use
metrics.question: Where does a larger share of people use the internet?
metrics.definition: Individuals who used the internet from any location in the past three months, as a percentage of the population.
metrics.sourceName: World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database, International Telecommunication Union (ITU), uri: https://datahub.itu.int/
metrics.sourceDefinition: Internet users are individuals who have used the Internet (from any location) in the last 3 months. The Internet can be used via a computer, mobile phone, personal digital assistant, games machine, digital TV etc.

metrics.label: Age 65 and over
metrics.question: Which country has a larger share of people aged 65 or over?
metrics.definition: People aged 65 and over as a percentage of the total population, using midyear estimates.
metrics.sourceName: World Population Prospects, United Nations (UN), publisher: UN Population Division
metrics.sourceDefinition: Population ages 65 and above as a percentage of the total population. Population is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship.

metrics.label: Life expectancy
metrics.question: Which country has a higher life expectancy at birth?
metrics.definition: Years a newborn would be expected to live if prevailing age-specific mortality patterns stayed the same throughout their life. This is a period measure, not an individual prediction.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Life expectancy at birth indicates the number of years a newborn infant would live if prevailing patterns of mortality at the time of its birth were to stay the same throughout its life.

metrics.label: Renewable electricity
metrics.question: Which country generates a larger share of its electricity from renewables?
metrics.definition: Electricity generated from renewable sources as a percentage of total electricity output. This measures generation, not total energy use or electricity consumption.
metrics.sourceName: IEA Energy Statistics Data Browser, International Energy Agency (IEA), uri: https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-tools/energy-statistics-data-browser, publisher: International Energy Agency (IEA), date accessed: 2025-03-25
metrics.sourceDefinition: Renewable electricity is the share of electricity generated by renewable power plants in total electricity generated by all types of plants.

metrics.label: Agricultural land
metrics.question: Which country uses a larger share of its land for agriculture?
metrics.definition: Agricultural land as a percentage of land area. Includes arable land, permanent crops, and permanent pastures.
metrics.sourceName: FAO electronic files and web site, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Agricultural land refers to the share of land area that is arable, under permanent crops, and under permanent pastures. Arable land includes land defined by the FAO as land under temporary crops (double-cropped areas are counted once), temporary meadows for mowing or for pasture, land under market or kitchen gardens, and land temporarily fallow. Land abandoned as a result of shifting cultivation is excluded. Land under permanent crops is land cultivated with crops that occupy the land for long periods and need not be replanted after each harvest, such as cocoa, coffee, and rubber. This category includes land under flowering shrubs, fruit trees, nut trees, and vines, but excludes land under trees grown for wood or timber. Permanent pasture is land used for five or more years for forage, including natural and cultivated crops.

metrics.label: Fish catches
metrics.question: Which country catches more fish?
metrics.definition: Capture fisheries production: the weight of catches landed by a country for commercial, industrial, recreational, and subsistence purposes. Includes inland and marine fishing. Farmed fish are counted separately and are not included here.
metrics.sourceName: Food and Agriculture Organization., Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Capture fisheries production measures the volume of fish catches landed by a country for all commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes.

metrics.label: Land area
metrics.question: Which country has more land?
metrics.definition: Land area in square kilometers. Excludes inland water bodies, continental-shelf claims, and exclusive economic zones. The country silhouettes are not drawn to a shared scale.
metrics.sourceName: FAOSTAT, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), uri: https://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/RL, publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Land area is a country's total area, excluding area under inland water bodies, national claims to continental shelf, and exclusive economic zones. In most cases the definition of inland water bodies includes major rivers and lakes.

metrics.label: Children per woman
metrics.question: Which country has a higher fertility rate?
metrics.definition: The number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if that year’s age-specific birth rates stayed the same. This is a population measure, not the average number of children already born to women today.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Total fertility rate represents the number of children that would be born to a woman if she were to live to the end of her childbearing years and bear children in accordance with age-specific fertility rates of the specified year.

metrics.label: Protected land
metrics.question: Which country protects a larger share of its land?
metrics.definition: The share of land in nationally designated protected areas of at least 1,000 hectares, including national parks and nature reserves. Excludes marine areas and sites protected only under local or provincial law.
metrics.sourceName:
Protected Planet: The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) and World Database on Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (WD-OECM), UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), uri: https://www.protectedplanet.net/en, publisher: Protected Planet, date accessed: 20240516, date published: 202405;
International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), uri: https://www.protectedplanet.net/en, publisher: Protected Planet, date accessed: 20240516
metrics.sourceDefinition: Terrestrial protected areas are totally or partially protected areas of at least 1,000 hectares that are designated by national authorities as scientific reserves with limited public access, national parks, natural monuments, nature reserves or wildlife sanctuaries, protected landscapes, and areas managed mainly for sustainable use. Marine areas, unclassified areas, littoral (intertidal) areas, and sites protected under local or provincial law are excluded.

metrics.label: Women in parliament
metrics.question: Where do women hold a larger share of seats in parliament?
metrics.definition: The percentage of seats held by women in the single or lower chamber of the national parliament. Upper chambers are not included.
metrics.sourceName: Monthly ranking of women in national parliaments, Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), uri: https://data.ipu.org/women-ranking/, note: For the year of 1998, the data is as of August 10, 1998., type: Excel, date accessed: 2026-03-29
metrics.sourceDefinition: Women in parliaments are the percentage of parliamentary seats in a single or lower chamber held by women.

metrics.label: Energy per person
metrics.question: Which country uses more energy per person?
metrics.definition: Primary energy use divided by population, expressed in kilograms of oil equivalent so different fuels can be compared. Includes industry and transport as well as households; it does not mean that much oil was actually burned.
metrics.sourceName: IEA Energy Statistics Data Browser, International Energy Agency (IEA), uri: https://www.iea.org/data-and-statistics/data-tools/energy-statistics-data-browser, publisher: International Energy Agency (IEA), date accessed: 2025-03-25
metrics.sourceDefinition: Energy use refers to use of primary energy before transformation to other end-use fuels, which is equal to indigenous production plus imports and stock changes, minus exports and fuels supplied to ships and aircraft engaged in international transport.

metrics.label: GDP per person
metrics.question: Which country has a higher GDP per person?
metrics.definition: Economic output per person, adjusted for differences in purchasing power and expressed in current international dollars. This is not a typical person’s income, salary, or wealth.
metrics.sourceDefinition:
This indicator provides values for gross domestic product (GDP) per person expressed in current international dollars, converted by purchasing power parities (PPPs). PPPs account for the different price levels across countries and thus PPP-based comparisons of economic output are more appropriate for comparing the output of economies and the average material well-being of their inhabitants than exchange-rate based comparisons.  

Gross domestic product is the total income earned through the production of goods and services in an economic territory during an accounting period. It can be measured in three different ways: using either the expenditure approach, the income approach, or the production approach. This series has been linked to produce a consistent time series to counteract breaks in series over time due to changes in base years, source data and methodologies. Thus, it may not be comparable with other national accounts series in the database for historical years. The core indicator has been divided by the general population to achieve a per capita estimate. This indicator is expressed in current prices, meaning no adjustment has been made to account for price changes over time. The PPP conversion factor is a currency conversion factor and a spatial price deflator. PPPs convert different currencies to a common currency and, in the process of conversion, equalize their purchasing power by eliminating the differences in price levels between countries, thereby allowing volume or output comparisons of GDP and its expenditure components.

metrics.label: Mobile subscriptions
metrics.question: Which country has more mobile phone subscriptions per person?
metrics.definition: Active mobile subscriptions with voice service per 100 people, including prepaid and postpaid plans. People can have several subscriptions, so the figure can exceed 100. This does not count unique phone owners.
metrics.sourceName: World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database, International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Mobile cellular telephone subscriptions are subscriptions to a public mobile telephone service that provide access to the PSTN using cellular technology. The indicator includes (and is split into) the number of postpaid subscriptions, and the number of active prepaid accounts (i.e. that have been used during the last three months). The indicator applies to all mobile cellular subscriptions that offer voice communications. It excludes subscriptions via data cards or USB modems, subscriptions to public mobile data services, private trunked mobile radio, telepoint, radio paging and telemetry services.

metrics.label: Freshwater per person
metrics.question: Which country has more renewable freshwater per person?
metrics.definition: Long-term average annual river flows and groundwater generated within the country, divided by the population in the data year. Excludes water flowing in from other countries. It measures natural resources, not access to drinking water.
metrics.sourceName: AQUASTAT - FAO's Global Information System on Water and Agriculture, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), uri: https://data.apps.fao.org/aquastat/, publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), date accessed: 20240529
metrics.sourceDefinition: Renewable internal freshwater resources flows refer to internal renewable resources (internal river flows and groundwater from rainfall) in the country. Renewable internal freshwater resources per capita are calculated using the World Bank's population estimates.

metrics.label: Fixed broadband
metrics.question: Which country has more fixed broadband connections per person?
metrics.definition: Fixed broadband subscriptions per 100 people, including homes and organizations. Excludes mobile-cellular data connections. Connections can be shared, and the source’s threshold is at least 256 kbit/s; this does not measure internet speed.
metrics.sourceName: World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database, International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Fixed broadband subscriptions refers to fixed subscriptions to high-speed access to the public Internet (a TCP/IP connection), at downstream speeds equal to, or greater than, 256 kbit/s. This includes cable modem, DSL, fiber-to-the-home/building, other fixed (wired)-broadband subscriptions, satellite broadband and terrestrial fixed wireless broadband. This total is measured irrespective of the method of payment. It excludes subscriptions that have access to data communications (including the Internet) via mobile-cellular networks. It should include fixed WiMAX and any other fixed wireless technologies. It includes both residential subscriptions and subscriptions for organizations.

metrics.label: Bank & mobile-money accounts
metrics.question: Where do more adults have a bank or mobile-money account?
metrics.definition: People aged 15 or over who report owning an account at a bank or other financial institution, alone or jointly, or personally using a mobile-money service in the past year. Based on survey responses.
metrics.sourceName: Global Findex Database, World Bank (WB), uri: https://www.worldbank.org/en/publication/globalfindex
metrics.sourceDefinition: Account denotes the percentage of respondents who report having an account (by themselves or together with someone else) at a bank or another type of financial institution or report personally using a mobile money service in the past 12 months (% age 15+).

metrics.label: Rain & snow
metrics.question: Which country gets more rain and snow in an average year?
metrics.definition: Long-term average annual precipitation across the country, including rain and the water equivalent of snow and other frozen precipitation. The source year identifies the dataset entry; it is not the weather observed in that particular year.
metrics.sourceName: FAOSTAT, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), publisher: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Average precipitation is the long-term average in depth (over space and time) of annual precipitation in the country. Precipitation is defined as any kind of water that falls from clouds as a liquid or a solid.

metrics.label: Tobacco use
metrics.question: Where does a larger share of adults use tobacco?
metrics.definition: Current tobacco use among people aged 15 or over, including smoked and smokeless tobacco, daily or occasionally. Excludes e-cigarettes. Rates are age-standardized to compare countries with different age structures.
metrics.sourceName: Global Health Observatory Data Repository, World Health Organization (WHO), uri: https://www.who.int/data/gho
metrics.sourceDefinition: The percentage of the population ages 15 years and over who currently use any tobacco product (smoked and/or smokeless tobacco) on a daily or non-daily basis. Tobacco products include cigarettes, pipes, cigars, cigarillos, waterpipes (hookah, shisha), bidis, kretek, heated tobacco products, and all forms of smokeless (oral and nasal) tobacco. Tobacco products exclude e-cigarettes (which do not contain tobacco), “e-cigars”, “e-hookahs”, JUUL and “e-pipes”. The rates are age-standardized to the WHO Standard Population.

metrics.label: Air pollution
metrics.question: Where are people exposed to more fine-particle air pollution?
metrics.definition: Mean annual exposure to outdoor PM2.5: particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers. Concentrations are weighted by where people live, including urban and rural areas. A higher value means more pollution, not better air.
metrics.sourceName: Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) Air Pollution Exposure Estimates and Risk Curves 1990-2023, GBD Collaborator Network, uri: https://ghdx.healthdata.org/record/ihme-data/gbd-2023-air-pollution-exposure-estimates-1990-2023, note: Need to create account to retrieve data., publisher: Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), date accessed: 2026-04-03, date published: 2026-01-23
metrics.sourceDefinition: Population-weighted exposure to ambient PM2.5 pollution is defined as the average level of exposure of a nation's population to concentrations of suspended particles measuring less than 2.5 microns in aerodynamic diameter, which are capable of penetrating deep into the respiratory tract and causing severe health damage. Exposure is calculated by weighting mean annual concentrations of PM2.5 by population in both urban and rural areas.

metrics.label: Children under 15
metrics.question: Which country has a larger share of children under 15?
metrics.definition: Children aged 0 through 14 as a percentage of the total resident population. This measures the share of children, not their total number.
metrics.sourceName: United Nations Population Division. World Population Prospects., United Nations Population Division, uri: https://population.un.org/wpp/, publisher: United Nations Population Division
metrics.sourceDefinition: Population between the ages 0 to 14 as a percentage of the total population. Population is based on the de facto definition of population.

metrics.label: International migrants
metrics.question: Where do international migrants make up more of the population?
metrics.definition: The share of residents born in another country, including refugees. Some countries use foreign citizenship as a proxy when birthplace data are unavailable. Source estimates may be modeled. This measures residents, not arrivals during the year.
metrics.sourceName: International Migrant Stock, United Nations (UN), publisher: UN Population Division
metrics.sourceDefinition: International migrant stock (% of population) is the proportion of people at mid-year born in a country other than that in which they live. It also includes refugees.

metrics.label: Patent applications
metrics.question: Where do residents file more patent applications per person?
metrics.definition: Patent applications filed by resident applicants at their home patent office, per million people. We divide by the same country’s population in the same year. Counts applications, not grants; overseas filings are excluded. Filing practices differ across countries.
metrics.sourceName: WIPO Patent Report: Statistics on Worldwide Patent Activity, World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), note: The International Bureau of WIPO assumes no responsibility with respect to the transformation of these data.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Patent applications are worldwide patent applications filed through the Patent Cooperation Treaty procedure or with a national patent office for exclusive rights for an invention--a product or process that provides a new way of doing something or offers a new technical solution to a problem. A patent provides protection for the invention to the owner of the patent for a limited period, generally 20 years.

metrics.label: Self-employment
metrics.question: Where is a larger share of workers self-employed?
metrics.definition: Self-employed workers as a share of all employed people, using modeled ILO estimates. Includes employers, people working for themselves, cooperative members, and contributing family workers; it is broader than freelancers or business founders.
metrics.sourceName: ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST), International Labour Organization (ILO), uri: https://ilostat.ilo.org/data/bulk/, publisher: ILOSTAT, type: external database, date accessed: January 17, 2026
metrics.sourceDefinition: Self-employed workers are those workers who, working on their own account or with one or a few partners or in cooperative, hold the type of jobs defined as a "self-employment jobs." i.e. jobs where the remuneration is directly dependent upon the profits derived from the goods and services produced. Self-employed workers include sub-categories of employers, own-account workers and members of producers' cooperatives and contributing family workers.

metrics.label: Population growth
metrics.question: Which country has a higher population growth rate?
metrics.definition: The annual change in the resident population, expressed as an exponential growth rate. Includes the combined effects of births, deaths, and migration. Negative values mean the population shrank.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Annual population growth rate for year t is the exponential rate of growth of midyear population from year t-1 to t, expressed as a percentage. Population is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship.

metrics.label: Birth rate
metrics.question: Which country has more births per person?
metrics.definition: Live births during the year per 1,000 residents, using the midyear population. Unlike fertility per woman, this rate also reflects the country’s age structure.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Crude birth rate indicates the number of live births occurring during the year, per 1,000 population estimated at midyear. Subtracting the crude death rate from the crude birth rate provides the rate of natural increase, which is equal to the rate of population change in the absence of migration.

metrics.label: Women & girls
metrics.question: Which country has a larger share of women and girls?
metrics.definition: Female residents as a share of the total population, using the source’s population estimates. Includes girls as well as adults and counts residents regardless of citizenship.
metrics.sourceName:
World Population Prospects, United Nations (UN), publisher: UN Population Division;
Staff estimates, World Bank (WB), note: World Bank staff estimates based on age/sex distributions of United Nations Population Division's World Population Prospects: 2022 Revision
metrics.sourceDefinition: Female population is the percentage of the population that is female. Population is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship.

metrics.label: Size of the economy
metrics.question: Which country has the larger economy?
metrics.definition: Total annual economic output, measured as GDP in current US dollars at market exchange rates. This is the size of the whole economy, not output per person, household wealth, or purchasing-power-adjusted GDP.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Gross domestic product is the total income earned through the production of goods and services in an economic territory during an accounting period. It can be measured in three different ways: using either the expenditure approach, the income approach, or the production approach. This indicator is expressed in current prices, meaning no adjustment has been made to account for price changes over time. This indicator is expressed in United States dollars.

metrics.label: Economic growth
metrics.question: Which country has a higher economic growth rate?
metrics.definition: Annual growth in real GDP: total economic output adjusted for price changes. Negative values mean the economy contracted. This measures growth during the stated year, not the size of the economy.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Gross domestic product is the total income earned through the production of goods and services in an economic territory during an accounting period. It can be measured in three different ways: using either the expenditure approach, the income approach, or the production approach. This indicator denotes the percentage change over each previous year of the constant price (base year 2015) series in United States dollars.

metrics.label: Inflation
metrics.question: Which country has a higher inflation rate?
metrics.definition: Annual change in the consumer price index, based on a basket of goods and services. This measures how fast prices changed during the stated year, not which country is more expensive. Negative values mean average consumer prices fell.
metrics.sourceName: International Financial Statistics database, International Monetary Fund (IMF)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Inflation as measured by the consumer price index reflects the annual percentage change in the cost to the average consumer of acquiring a basket of goods and services that may be fixed or changed at specified intervals, such as yearly.

metrics.label: Unemployment
metrics.question: Which country has a higher unemployment rate?
metrics.definition: People without work who are available for and seeking employment, as a share of the labor force. People not seeking work are outside this denominator. Uses modeled ILO estimates.
metrics.sourceName: ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST), International Labour Organization (ILO), uri: https://ilostat.ilo.org/data/bulk/, publisher: ILOSTAT, type: external database, date accessed: January 17, 2026
metrics.sourceDefinition: Unemployment refers to the share of the labor force that is without work but available for and seeking employment.

metrics.label: Women in the workforce
metrics.question: Where are more women working or looking for work?
metrics.definition: Women aged 15 or over who are employed or unemployed and actively participating in the labor force, as a share of all women in that age group. Uses modeled ILO estimates; this is not the share of workers who are women.
metrics.sourceName: ILO Modelled Estimates database (ILOEST), International Labour Organization (ILO), uri: https://ilostat.ilo.org/data/bulk/, publisher: ILOSTAT, type: external database, date accessed: January 17, 2026
metrics.sourceDefinition: The labor force participation rate is the labor force as a percent of the population ages 15 and older. The labor force is the sum of all persons of working age who are employed and those who are unemployed.

metrics.label: Military spending
metrics.question: Which country spends a larger share of its economy on the military?
metrics.definition: Military expenditure as a percentage of GDP, using SIPRI’s estimates. Includes military personnel, operations, procurement, and military research. This is a share of the economy, not the share of the government budget.
metrics.sourceName: SIPRI Military Expenditure Database, Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), uri: https://www.sipri.org/databases
metrics.sourceDefinition: Military expenditure by country as percentage of gross domestic product

metrics.label: Research & development
metrics.question: Which country spends a larger share of its economy on research?
metrics.definition: Domestic spending on research and development as a share of GDP. Includes businesses, government, universities, and private nonprofits, and covers basic research, applied research, and experimental development.
metrics.sourceName: Stat Bulk Data Download Service, UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), uri: https://databrowser.uis.unesco.org/resources/bulk, publisher: UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), date accessed: 2025-03-26, date published: 2025-02
metrics.sourceDefinition: Gross domestic expenditures on research and development (R&D), expressed as a percent of GDP. They include both capital and current expenditures in the four main sectors: Business enterprise, Government, Higher education and Private non-profit. R&D covers basic research, applied research, and experimental development.

metrics.label: Researchers
metrics.question: Which country has more researchers per person?
metrics.definition: Researchers engaged in research and development per million residents, measured in full-time-equivalent roles. Includes relevant postgraduate researchers. This measures time spent doing research, not a headcount of everyone with a science degree.
metrics.sourceName: Stat Bulk Data Download Service, UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), uri: https://databrowser.uis.unesco.org/resources/bulk, publisher: UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), date accessed: 2025-03-26, date published: 2025-02
metrics.sourceDefinition: The number of researchers engaged in Research &Development (R&D), expressed as per million. Researchers are professionals who conduct research and improve or develop concepts, theories, models techniques instrumentation, software of operational methods. R&D covers basic research, applied research, and experimental development.

metrics.label: Scientific publications
metrics.question: Which country produces more scientific papers per person?
metrics.definition: Science and engineering journal articles and conference papers indexed by Scopus, divided by the same country’s population in the same year. International coauthors split publication credit between countries. Coverage is not every paper or every academic field.
metrics.sourceName: Science and Engineering Indicators, National Science Foundation (NSF), uri: https://ncses.nsf.gov/indicators
metrics.sourceDefinition: Article counts refer to publications from a selection of conference proceedings and peer-reviewed journals from Scopus in science and engineering fields, according to the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics Taxonomy of Disciplines.

metrics.label: Education spending
metrics.question: Which country puts a larger share of its economy into public education?
metrics.definition: Government expenditure on education as a share of GDP, including current spending, capital spending, and transfers. Covers local, regional, and central government. Private household spending is not included.
metrics.sourceName: Data API, UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), uri: https://databrowser.uis.unesco.org/resources, note: The data are obtained through the UIS API.  Detailed documentation is available at: https://api.uis.unesco.org/api/public/documentation/, publisher: UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), date accessed: 2026-03-19, date published: 2026-02
metrics.sourceDefinition: General government expenditure on education (current, capital, and transfers) is expressed as a percentage of GDP. It includes expenditure funded by transfers from international sources to government. General government usually refers to local, regional and central governments.

metrics.label: Healthcare spending
metrics.question: Which country spends a larger share of its economy on healthcare?
metrics.definition: Current spending on healthcare goods and services as a share of GDP, including public and private spending. Excludes capital investments such as hospital buildings and major equipment. Higher spending does not by itself measure better care.
metrics.sourceName: Global Health Expenditure Database, updated December 12th, 2025, World Health Organization (WHO), uri: https://apps.who.int/nha/database
metrics.sourceDefinition: Level of current health expenditure expressed as a percentage of GDP.  Estimates of current health expenditures include healthcare goods and services consumed during each year. This indicator does not include capital health expenditures such as buildings, machinery, IT and stocks of vaccines for emergency or outbreaks.

metrics.label: Doctors
metrics.question: Which country has more doctors per person?
metrics.definition: Generalist and specialist medical practitioners per 1,000 residents. Reporting and training definitions vary between countries. This national average does not show how evenly doctors are distributed within the country.
metrics.sourceDefinition: Physicians include generalist and specialist medical practitioners.

metrics.label: Hospital beds
metrics.question: Which country has more hospital beds per person?
metrics.definition: Inpatient beds in public, private, general, and specialized hospitals and rehabilitation centers, per 1,000 residents. Usually includes both acute and chronic care. Bed counts do not measure the quality or availability of treatment.
metrics.sourceName: WHO data, supplemented by country data, World Health Organization (WHO)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Hospital beds include inpatient beds available in public, private, general, and specialized hospitals and rehabilitation centers. In most cases beds for both acute and chronic care are included.

metrics.label: Landline subscriptions
metrics.question: Which country has more landline subscriptions per person?
metrics.definition: Fixed telephone subscriptions per 100 residents, including conventional lines, fixed VoIP services, and public payphones. Includes homes and organizations; it does not count unique people or mobile subscriptions.
metrics.sourceName: World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators Database, International Telecommunication Union (ITU)
metrics.sourceDefinition: Fixed telephone subscriptions refers to the sum of active number of analogue fixed telephone lines, voice-over-IP (VoIP) subscriptions, fixed wireless local loop (WLL) subscriptions, ISDN voice-channel equivalents and fixed public payphones.

metrics.label: Safe drinking water
metrics.question: Where do more people have safely managed drinking water?
metrics.definition: People using an improved drinking-water source that is on their premises, available when needed, and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. The measure requires all three conditions, not just a piped connection.

WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene, World Health Organization (WHO), uri: washdata.org, note: Aggregate data by groups are computed based on the groupings for the World Bank fiscal year in which the data was released by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene., publisher: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (washdata.org), date accessed: 2025-09-30, date published: 2025-08-25;
UN Children's Fund (UNICEF), uri: washdata.org, note: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene
metrics.sourceDefinition: The percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged or delivered water.

metrics.label: Sanitation
metrics.question: Where do more people have basic sanitation at home?
metrics.definition: People using improved sanitation facilities that are not shared with other households. Includes flush toilets, suitable pit latrines, and composting toilets, as well as safely managed sanitation. Shared facilities do not qualify as basic under this measure.
metrics.sourceName:
WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene, World Health Organization (WHO), uri: washdata.org, publisher: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (washdata.org), date accessed: 2025-09-30, date published: 2025-08-25;
UN Children's Fund (UNICEF), uri: washdata.org, note: WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene
metrics.sourceDefinition: The percentage of people using at least basic sanitation services, that is, improved sanitation facilities that are not shared with other households.  This indicator encompasses both people using basic sanitation services as well as those using safely managed sanitation services.   Improved sanitation facilities include flush/pour flush to piped sewer systems, septic tanks or pit latrines; ventilated improved pit latrines, composting toilets or pit latrines with slabs.
